steps.prompt: Let $p(x) = x^2 + x + 1$. Work out $p(2)$. Now: $x^2 + x + 1 = (x - 2)(x + 3) + 7$. What do you notice?

cards.title: The remainder theorem
cards.body: Dividing $p(x)$ by $x - a$ gives $p(x) = (x - a)q(x) + R$. Put $x = a$ in: the first part is $0$, so $R = p(a)$. The remainder is just $p(a)$, no long division needed. If $p(a) = 0$, then $x - a$ is a FACTOR of $p(x)$.

cards.title: Worked example: plug in
cards.problem: What is the remainder when $x^3 - 4x^2 + 2x + 7$ is divided by $x - 3$?

steps.text: Dividing by $x - 3$ means $a = 3$: the remainder is $p(3)$.

cards.title: Handy values
cards.body: Dividing by $x + 2$ means $a = -2$. Dividing by $2x - 1$ means $x = \frac{1}{2}$. $p(1)$ is the SUM of the coefficients, $p(0)$ is the constant term, and $p(-1)$ is the alternating sum. Dividing by a quadratic leaves a remainder like $ax + b$.

cards.title: Worked example: make it a factor
cards.problem: For what value of $k$ is $x - 2$ a factor of $x^3 + kx - 6$?

cards.title: The common trap: the sign of a
cards.body: Dividing by $x + 2$: plug in $-2$, not $2$. Set the divisor equal to zero and solve for $x$; that is the number to plug in. And a remainder of $0$ means "is a factor", not "no answer".

prompts: What number do you plug in to find the remainder when dividing by $x + 5$? By $3x - 2$? How do you know?
